full_prose_under_review.title: Supplying Patients Beyond the Pharmacy Counter: Off-Site Processing, Central Fill, Delivery, Lock Boxes, Emergency Kits and Hospice Acute Use
full_prose_under_review.topic: Pharmacy operations / Supply of prescriptions and drugs outside the dispensing pharmacy's own counter
full_prose_under_review.subtopic: Off-site processing under 247 CMR 9.04(11); shared pharmacy services, remote processing, telepharmacy and central fill under Board Policy 2021-02 with the DEA central fill rules in 21 CFR 1300.01, 1304.05, 1306.14(b), 1306.15, 1306.24(b) and 1306.27; mail and common carrier delivery under 247 CMR 9.02 and the Board's delivery and shipping advisory; bed-side delivery and workplace collection under 247 CMR 9.04(4) and (9); prescription lock boxes under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21B; long-term care facility emergency kits under 247 CMR 9.09, 105 CMR 150.008(E) and Circular Letter DHCQ 18-6-679; and hospice inpatient acute-use medications under Circular Letter DHCQ 20-3-700
learning_objectives: Apply the two alternative conditions in 247 CMR 9.04(11) to medication processed outside the dispensing pharmacy, and distinguish remote processing from telepharmacy under Policy 2021-02.
State the general safeguards Policy 2021-02 imposes on every shared pharmacy service model, including ownership or agreement, patient notice and opt-out, and the annual documented policy review.
Decide where a centrally filled prescription may go by schedule and monitoring-program status, which pharmacies may act as central fill pharmacies, and what may not be centrally filled.
Assign the federal central fill marking, record, retention and label duties to the retail pharmacy or the central fill pharmacy, and explain how Board policy extends that handling to Schedule VI.
Separate the binding sentences of 247 CMR 9.02 from the recommendations in the Board's delivery and shipping advisory.
Apply the conditions for bed-side delivery in 247 CMR 9.04(4) and for workplace collection in 247 CMR 9.04(9).
State which pharmacies must sell lock boxes under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21B and the placement, size and wording of the sign.
Apply the pharmacy, facility and circular-letter requirements for long-term care facility emergency kits, including the bed-band caps and the 48-hour reseal.
Apply the hospice acute-use pathway: its purpose limit, registration and monitoring, category caps, ownership and reconciliation.

orientation.text: This section follows a prescription or a dose that reaches a patient by some route other than the dispensing pharmacy's own counter. Two layers of Massachusetts text govern those routes, and they must be kept apart. The binding layer is statute and regulation: 247 CMR 9.02 on prescriptions by mail, 247 CMR 9.04(4), (9) and (11) on bed-side delivery, workplace collection and off-site processing, 247 CMR 9.09 on emergency medication kits, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21B on lock boxes, and the Department's long-term care facility rule in 105 CMR 150.008(E). The guidance layer is the Board's Policy 2021-02 on shared pharmacy services (adopted 2/19/21, revised 4/7/22 and 2/6/25), the Board's Advisory on Medication Delivery and Shipping (adopted 6/28/18, revised 1/9/25), and two Department circular letters, DHCQ 18-6-679 on long-term care facility emergency kits (June 15, 2018) and DHCQ 20-3-700 on hospice inpatient acute-use medications (March 6, 2020). Where a centrally filled prescription is for a federally controlled substance, the DEA regulations bind as well, and where both a federal and a Massachusetts text reach the same act the pharmacy follows the stricter one.

The starting point for any work done away from the dispensing pharmacy is 247 CMR 9.04(11): a pharmacy may not dispense any medication that was processed outside its licensed pharmacy premises unless that process was verified by a Massachusetts licensed pharmacist or was performed in a pharmacy licensed by the Board. The two conditions are alternatives, and each attaches to the process, so the dispensing pharmacist's inspection of a finished product that arrives from an unlicensed site does not supply either one. Policy 2021-02 repeats the same two conditions for what it calls remote processing, which it defines as processing patient-specific prescriptions outside the licensed premises of a Massachusetts-licensed pharmacy without final product verification or dispensing responsibilities. The policy also allows telepharmacy, limited to remote pharmacist verification of final patient-specific products and clinical activities such as counseling, drug utilization review and drug therapy monitoring, conducted by a Massachusetts-licensed pharmacist or performed in a Board-licensed pharmacy, with at least one licensed pharmacist on the premises of the Board-licensed pharmacy that dispenses the final product and verification technology that meets the policy's image and data-retention minimums. What a technician may do in remote processing belongs to the section on pharmacy technicians, and counseling itself to the section on counseling.

Every shared pharmacy service model under Policy 2021-02 carries the same general safeguards. The participants must either have the same owner or have a written contract or agreement that outlines the services and each party's shared responsibilities; the services must occur within the United States; the participants share a common electronic file or technology with secure access, protect the confidentiality of protected health information, and may not duplicate, download or remove any part of the database; dispensing must be pursuant to valid patient-specific prescriptions or standing orders; the system must produce an audit trail showing at least the date, time and individuals involved at each step; and each participant is jointly responsible for properly processed and filled prescriptions. Retail pharmacies must tell patients that their prescriptions may be processed or filled by another pharmacy and give them a way to opt out. Training is documented, joint policies and procedures are written to at least the NABP Model Act's shared pharmacy services content and reviewed at least annually with the review documented, and a continuity of care plan covers a participant that cannot process or fill. A shared service model the policy does not address needs a petition to the Board for approval, unless the policy notes otherwise.

Central fill is the model in which one retail pharmacy receives a prescription and a second pharmacy prepares the filled prescription and delivers it back to the first pharmacy for dispensing to the patient. Under Policy 2021-02 retail pharmacies licensed by the Board may serve as central fill pharmacies for other Board-licensed retail pharmacies, one central fill pharmacy may serve more than one pharmacy, and any central fill pharmacy dispensing into, within or from Massachusetts must itself be licensed by Massachusetts as a resident or non-resident retail pharmacy. The policy then sorts by schedule. Centrally filled Schedule II through V controlled substances must be delivered to the pharmacy where the prescription originated for final dispensing to the patient, and participating pharmacies that dispense them must follow the DEA central fill regulations and be registered with DEA. Massachusetts Schedule VI prescriptions are handled in the same manner as those DEA regulations outline, except that the phrase "central fill" need not be added to a Schedule VI prescription and a centrally filled Schedule VI drug may be delivered or shipped directly to the patient from the central fill pharmacy, unless it is a drug, such as gabapentin, that must be reported to the Prescription Monitoring Program. Central filling of compounded sterile preparations or complex non-sterile preparations to be dispensed into, within or from Massachusetts is prohibited, and participants keep a policy and procedure for medications never dispensed to patients. Licensure of non-resident pharmacies as such belongs to the facility licensure section.

The federal rules a Massachusetts pharmacy needs for a controlled-substance central fill are few and precise. A central fill pharmacy under 21 CFR 1300.01 is one permitted by its state to prepare controlled substance orders on a valid prescription transmitted by a registered retail pharmacy and to return the labeled and filled prescription to that retail pharmacy for delivery to the ultimate user, and it is authorized to fill for that retail pharmacy only if the two have a contractual relationship or share a common owner. A retail pharmacy registration permits central fill activity, only a pharmacist in a registered pharmacy, registered central fill pharmacy or registered institutional practitioner may fill, and the corresponding liability for filling a prescription not in proper form reaches a pharmacist employed by a central fill pharmacy. Under 21 CFR 1306.15 for Schedule II and 1306.27 for Schedules III through V, the retail pharmacy may transmit the prescription electronically, including by fax; it writes "CENTRAL FILL" on the face of the original prescription and records the central fill pharmacy's name, address and DEA number, its own transmitting pharmacist and the date, sends everything 21 CFR 1306.05 requires (and, for Schedules III through V, the refills dispensed and remaining), keeps the original for two years from filling (Schedule II) or from the last refill (Schedules III through V), and records receipt of the filled prescription, the delivery method and the employee who accepted it. The central fill pharmacy keeps what it received, the date of receipt, the filling pharmacist and the filling dates, and when and how it delivered the filled prescription back. It also affixes a label showing the retail pharmacy's name and address and a unique identifier such as its own DEA number, and each pharmacy keeps a list of its partners with their DEA numbers and verifies their registrations. A central fill pharmacy may not prepare a Schedule II prescription on an oral authorization, a delivery from a central fill pharmacy to a retail pharmacy needs no DEA Form 222, and when a retail pharmacy contracts the carrier that retrieves filled prescriptions it reports in-transit losses itself.

Mail and common carrier delivery sit in 247 CMR 9.02, which has three sentences with three different functions. A pharmacy and pharmacist may dispense prescription drugs by mail or common carrier in a manner consistent with federal and state law; the pharmacy shall ensure that packing, shipping and transportation processes do not adversely affect the integrity or stability of medications dispensed by mail; and the pharmacy shall maintain policies and procedures regarding packing, shipping, transporting and delivering controlled substances. The Board's Advisory on Medication Delivery and Shipping sits on top of that as best practice recommendations the Board urges pharmacies to consider: patient consent, a documented workflow, trained packaging staff, two employees witnessing controlled substance packaging, a signature on delivery and a tracking number for Schedule II through V packages with the pharmacy's address but not its name on the label, transport time-test studies at least twice a year for temperature-sensitive products, and policies for hazardous products, unclaimed packages, losses in transit and contracted drivers. The advisory also states that a specialty pharmacy delivering to a retail pharmacy for patient pick-up may do so only with the final packaged product, which the receiving pharmacy may not alter. Cold-chain storage standards belong to the section on returns, recalls and product integrity, and the counseling route for delivered prescriptions to the counseling section.

Two provisions in 247 CMR 9.04 govern delivery to people in particular places. Under 9.04(4) a pharmacy that provides bed-side delivery of discharge prescriptions to patients in an inpatient healthcare facility must obtain patient consent, may not restrict the patient's freedom of choice of pharmacy services, and shall deliver the medications directly to the patient or the patient's agent. Under 9.04(9) a pharmacist or a person acting for a pharmacy may not collect prescriptions at industrial plants, places of business or other sites where specific groups of people are regularly employed or affiliated unless every listed condition is met: the prescriptions are for people regularly employed at or affiliated with the site or for immediate family members living at the same address as those people; a pharmacist, pharmacy employee or authorized agent collects them in person and dispenses the medications directly to the patient or the patient's agent; everything not so handed over is returned to the pharmacy and nothing is left or stored at the delivery location; and the pharmacist and pharmacy are responsible for the conduct of the employee or agent. Under 9.04(15) neither paragraph applies to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies. Separately, M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21B requires a pharmacy registered in the commonwealth to dispense Schedule II, III, IV or V prescription drugs to make prescription lock boxes available for sale at each store location and to display, on or near the pharmacy counter, a sign at least 4 inches by 5 inches stating in legible print that lock boxes for securing prescription medications are available at the pharmacy; the statute's definition of pharmacy excludes an institutional pharmacy or pharmacy department except as 247 CMR provides.

Emergency medication kits in long-term care facilities are governed at three levels. The Board's 247 CMR 9.09 binds the supplying pharmacy: it maintains a policy and procedure for dispensing through kits covering security, maintenance and use, reconciles medication dispensed through kits with prescriptions or orders, and may provide kits only to types of facilities the Board has approved. The Department's 105 CMR 150.008(E) binds the facility: a kit shall be provided in every facility, its contents are approved by the Department, it is kept in a separate sealed container (with refrigerated drugs in a separate sealed refrigerated container), it is prepared, packaged and sealed by a pharmacist with a contents list outside and inside, its medications are used only on a primary care provider's order, and after opening the pharmacist inspects, re-stocks and reseals it within 48 hours prior to further use. Circular Letter DHCQ 18-6-679, issued under 105 CMR 150.008(E)(1), sets the controlled substance framework: a facility may choose Schedule II through V analgesics and sedatives or anticonvulsants up to per-facility unit caps set by licensed bed capacity in a 3:1 ratio (45 and 15 units under 50 beds, 60 and 20 for 51 to 100, 75 and 25 for 101 to 150, 90 and 30 above 150), each unit tamper evident or resistant and individually packaged in single-dose form; it should build its formulary with a single pharmacy provider of its choosing and keep accountability and security procedures; Schedule VI emergency doses carry full procurement-to-disposal requirements and monitoring by the facility's Quality Assurance and Assessment Committee; and an automated dispensing device may replace the traditional locked box for Schedule II through V, provided all relevant regulations and guidance requirements are met. The printed bands are fewer than 50 beds and 51 to 100 beds, so exactly 50 beds has no printed band; the circular does not resolve it, and the smaller caps are the course that is safe on either reading. How such a device is loaded and run belongs to the dispensing automation section.

Hospice inpatient facilities have a separate pathway in Circular Letter DHCQ 20-3-700. It lets the facility's pharmacy provider store certain non-patient-specific Schedule II through VI medications on site in an automated dispensing device for acute use, meaning symptoms that are not life threatening but need timely treatment for prompt palliative care, and the supply should only be enough to treat the patient until the pharmacy can fill and deliver the full prescription. The pharmacy must use a device, obtain a machine-specific Controlled Substance Registration from the Board, determine whether a machine-specific DEA number is required, and meet continuous video monitoring and the other device requirements of Policy 2019-02. The device may hold no more than the per-facility category caps: analgesics 50, 100 and 150 units; sedatives or anticonvulsants 30, 60 and 90; and Schedule VI ancillary medications such as antiemetics and antipsychotics 25, 50 and 75, in bands printed as fewer than 10 beds, 11 to 20 beds and more than 21 beds. The contents remain the pharmacy's property until dispensed for administration on a prescription or order, the pharmacy reconciles what the device dispenses with prescriptions, and every unit is tamper evident or resistant in individually packaged single-dose form. The printed bands leave exactly 10 and exactly 21 beds unassigned; the circular does not say which figure applies, so a facility of that size is safest keeping to the lower band's caps unless the Department confirms otherwise.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy uses a commonly owned central fill pharmacy that is licensed by the Board as a non-resident retail pharmacy. In one batch the central fill pharmacy prepares a morphine tablet prescription, a gabapentin prescription and a Schedule VI antihypertensive prescription, and proposes shipping all three straight to the patients' homes to save a day.
steps: Confirm the arrangement itself: common ownership satisfies the policy's ownership-or-agreement condition and the federal authorization condition, and the central fill pharmacy holds the Massachusetts retail licence the policy requires.

Morphine is a Schedule II controlled substance, so the policy requires the filled prescription to go to the pharmacy where the prescription originated for final dispensing, and the DEA definition likewise returns it to the retail pharmacy for delivery to the ultimate user.
Gabapentin is a Massachusetts Schedule VI drug that is reported to the Prescription Monitoring Program, and the policy names it as the example of a Schedule VI drug excluded from direct shipment.
The antihypertensive is Schedule VI and not reportable, so the policy allows the central fill pharmacy to deliver or ship it directly to the patient, subject to 247 CMR 9.02 for the shipment itself.
worked_examples.resolution: Only the non-reportable Schedule VI prescription may go directly to the patient; the morphine and gabapentin prescriptions must go back to the originating pharmacy. The error the scenario invites is treating a lawful central fill relationship, or Schedule VI status alone, as permission to ship every centrally filled prescription to the patient.

worked_examples.scenario: A retail pharmacy transmits a Schedule III prescription to its central fill pharmacy by fax. The transmitting pharmacist writes nothing on the original, assuming the central fill pharmacy will mark its own copy, and the retail pharmacy plans to discard the original two years after the first fill although the prescription has been refilled since.
steps: Under 21 CFR 1306.27(a)(1) it is the transmitting retail pharmacy that writes "CENTRAL FILL" on the face of the original and records the central fill pharmacy's name, address and DEA number, the transmitting pharmacist and the date of transmittal.
Because this is a Schedule III prescription, the transmission must also show the number of refills already dispensed and the number remaining under 1306.27(a)(3).

The original must be kept for two years from the date the prescription was last refilled under 1306.27(a)(4), not from the first fill; the from-filling measure belongs to Schedule II under 1306.15(a)(3).
The central fill pharmacy keeps its own records of the fax copy, receipt, filling pharmacist, filling and refilling dates and delivery back, which do not replace the retail pharmacy's.
worked_examples.resolution: The retail pharmacy must mark and annotate the original itself, send the refill counts, and keep the original two years from the last refill. The error invited is shifting the marking duty to the central fill pharmacy and borrowing the Schedule II retention trigger.

worked_examples.scenario: A 120-bed long-term care facility asks its pharmacy to stock its emergency kit with 80 Schedule II-V analgesic units, argues it may skip the sedative category and use that allowance for analgesics, and wants the charge nurse to reseal the kit after each use so it is back in service at once.
steps: Place the facility in its band: 120 licensed beds falls in the 101 to 150 band of Circular Letter DHCQ 18-6-679, so the caps are 75 analgesic units and 25 sedative/anticonvulsant units.

The circular sets a separate maximum number of units for each medication group per facility, so unused sedative/anticonvulsant capacity does not add to the analgesic maximum, and a facility need not stock the maximum in either group.

Under 105 CMR 150.008(E)(3) and (5) the kit is prepared, packaged and sealed by a pharmacist, and after opening it is inspected, re-stocked and resealed by the pharmacist within 48 hours prior to further use.
The supplying pharmacy must also reconcile what was dispensed from the kit with prescriptions or orders and keep its security, maintenance and use policy under 247 CMR 9.09.
worked_examples.resolution: The kit may hold at most 75 analgesic units, and resealing is the pharmacist's task, not the nurse's. The error invited is pooling the category caps and treating resealing as a facility nursing function.

worked_examples.scenario: An 18-bed hospice inpatient facility asks its pharmacy provider to add a locked box of hydromorphone and lorazepam at the nursing station, to keep the supply large enough that routine prescriptions rarely need to be filled, and to treat the stock as facility property once it arrives.
steps: Circular Letter DHCQ 20-3-700 requires the pharmacy provider to use an automated dispensing device, with a machine-specific Controlled Substance Registration, a determination whether a machine-specific DEA number is required, and continuous video monitoring; a locked box is not the pathway.

The purpose is acute use for non-life-threatening symptoms needing prompt palliation, and the supply should only be enough to treat the patient until the pharmacy can fill and deliver the full prescription.
At 18 beds the facility is in the 11 to 20 band, so the device may hold no more than 100 analgesic, 60 sedative/anticonvulsant and 50 Schedule VI ancillary units.
The contents remain the pharmacy's property until dispensed for administration on a prescription or order, and the pharmacy reconciles what is dispensed with prescriptions.
worked_examples.resolution: The request fails on storage method, purpose and ownership; a compliant arrangement is a registered device within the 11 to 20 bed caps that bridges only to the full prescription. The error invited is importing the long-term care locked-kit model into hospice and treating acute-use stock as floor stock.

worked_examples.scenario: A pharmacy offers a service at a large employer: a technician collects prescriptions in person at the plant on Monday and brings the filled medications back on Wednesday, leaving any that employees did not pick up with the plant's security desk until the following week. One prescription is for an employee's adult son who lives elsewhere.
steps: 247 CMR 9.04(9) allows collection at such a site only when every condition is met, and the prescriptions must be for people regularly employed at or affiliated with the site or for immediate family members living at the same address as those people.
The son lives at a different address, so his prescription does not qualify for collection at the plant.

The medications must be dispensed directly to the patient or the patient's agent, and all medications not handed over must be returned to the pharmacy; nothing may be left or stored at the delivery location.
The pharmacist and pharmacy are responsible for the conduct of the employee or agent running the service.
worked_examples.resolution: Leaving unclaimed medications at the security desk violates 9.04(9)(d), and the son's prescription may not be collected there. The error invited is treating a trusted workplace contact as a permissible holding point.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 247 CMR 9.04(11), on what two alternative conditions may a pharmacy dispense medication processed outside its licensed premises?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The process was verified by a Massachusetts licensed pharmacist, or it was performed in a pharmacy licensed by the Board.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under Policy 2021-02, where must a centrally filled Schedule II-V prescription be delivered?
retrieval_prompts.answer: To the pharmacy where the prescription originated, for final dispensing to the patient.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which centrally filled Schedule VI drugs may not be shipped directly to the patient under Policy 2021-02?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Drugs requiring reporting to the Prescription Monitoring Program, such as gabapentin.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What licence must a central fill pharmacy dispensing into, within or from Massachusetts hold under Policy 2021-02?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A Massachusetts resident or non-resident retail pharmacy licence.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which preparations may not be centrally filled for dispensing into, within or from Massachusetts?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Compounded sterile preparations and complex non-sterile preparations.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under Policy 2021-02, what two things must retail pharmacies offer patients about shared services?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Notice that their prescriptions may be processed or filled by another pharmacy, and a mechanism to opt out.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 21 CFR 1300.01, what relationship makes a central fill pharmacy authorized to fill for a retail pharmacy?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A contractual relationship providing for such activities, or a common owner.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who writes "CENTRAL FILL" on the original controlled-substance prescription, and what else is recorded?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The transmitting retail pharmacy, recording the central fill pharmacy's name, address and DEA number, the transmitting pharmacist and the date of transmittal.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How long does the retail pharmacy keep the original prescription sent for central fill, and from when?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Two years: from the date filled for Schedule II, and from the date last refilled for Schedules III-V.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What extra content does a central fill pharmacy's label on a controlled-substance prescription carry?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The retail pharmacy's name and address and a unique identifier, such as the central fill pharmacy's DEA registration number, showing it was filled there.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What does 247 CMR 9.02(3) require policies and procedures to address?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Packing, shipping, transporting and delivering controlled substances.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: To whom must a bed-side delivery of discharge prescriptions be handed?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Directly to the patient or the patient's agent, after obtaining patient consent and without restricting freedom of choice.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which pharmacies must sell lock boxes under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21B, and what sign is required?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A pharmacy registered in the commonwealth to dispense Schedule II-V prescription drugs, at each store location; a sign on or near the pharmacy counter at least 4 by 5 inches stating that lock boxes for securing prescription medications are available.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Within what period must an opened long-term care facility emergency kit be resealed, and by whom?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Inspected, re-stocked and resealed by the pharmacist within 48 hours prior to further use.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What are the emergency kit caps for a 60-bed long-term care facility?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 60 Schedule II-V analgesic units and 20 sedative/anticonvulsant units.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What are the hospice acute-use caps for a facility with fewer than 10 beds?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 50 analgesic, 30 sedative/anticonvulsant and 25 Schedule VI ancillary units.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who owns the medications in a hospice acute-use automated dispensing device before they are dispensed?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The pharmacy, until they are dispensed for administration pursuant to a prescription or order.

quick_review.text: Off-site processing is lawful for dispensing only if the process was verified by a Massachusetts licensed pharmacist or performed in a Board-licensed pharmacy.

Shared pharmacy service participants need the same owner or a written contract or agreement, a common secure system, an audit trail, documented training, joint policies reviewed at least annually, and a continuity of care plan.
Board-licensed retail pharmacies may serve as central fill pharmacies for other Board-licensed retail pharmacies.
Centrally filled Schedule II-V prescriptions return to the originating pharmacy; non-reportable Schedule VI prescriptions may be shipped directly to the patient.

Participating pharmacies dispensing Schedule II-V must follow the DEA central fill regulations and be DEA-registered, and Schedule VI is handled the same way except that the phrase "central fill" is not required.
Federally, the retail pharmacy marks and annotates the original and records receipt; the central fill pharmacy labels the package with the retail pharmacy's name and address and its own identifier.
247 CMR 9.02 permits mail and common carrier dispensing, requires integrity and stability in packing, shipping and transport, and requires controlled substance shipping policies.
The delivery and shipping advisory is a set of Board best practice recommendations, not regulation.
Bed-side discharge deliveries need patient consent, respect freedom of choice and go directly to the patient or agent.
Workplace collection requires eligible patients, in-person collection, direct hand-over and return of anything not handed over.
Lock boxes are for sale at each store location of a pharmacy registered to dispense Schedule II-V, with a sign of at least 4 by 5 inches on or near the counter.
Long-term care emergency kit caps run 45/60/75/90 analgesic and 15/20/25/30 sedative/anticonvulsant units by bed band.
Hospice acute-use caps run 50/100/150 analgesic, 30/60/90 sedative/anticonvulsant and 25/50/75 Schedule VI ancillary units by bed band.

decision_logic.condition: Any step of a prescription was processed outside the dispensing pharmacy's licensed premises.
decision_logic.action: Before dispensing, confirm the process was verified by a Massachusetts licensed pharmacist or performed in a Board-licensed pharmacy; a final check of the product does not substitute.

decision_logic.condition: Two pharmacies want to share processing, filling or verification.
decision_logic.action: Confirm common ownership or a written agreement, the policy's general safeguards, patient notice with opt-out, and that the model is one Policy 2021-02 addresses; otherwise petition the Board.

Confirm the central fill pharmacy is a Massachusetts-licensed retail pharmacy, that the preparation is not a compounded sterile or complex non-sterile preparation, and that both pharmacies are DEA-registered if Schedule II-V is involved.

decision_logic.condition: A centrally filled prescription is ready to leave the central fill pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Schedules II-V: send it to the originating pharmacy. Schedule VI reportable to the monitoring program: same. Other Schedule VI: it may go directly to the patient under 247 CMR 9.02.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule II-V prescription is transmitted for central fill.
decision_logic.action: Retail pharmacy marks "CENTRAL FILL", records the central fill pharmacy and transmittal details, sends the required prescription information (with refill counts for III-V) and keeps the original two years; central fill pharmacy keeps its receipt, filling and delivery records and labels the package.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription will be mailed or sent by common carrier.
decision_logic.action: Protect integrity and stability through packing, shipping and transport; for a controlled substance, follow the pharmacy's written procedures; consider the advisory's recommendations.

decision_logic.condition: Discharge prescriptions will be delivered to an inpatient's bedside.
decision_logic.action: Obtain the patient's consent, do not restrict pharmacy choice, and hand the medications to the patient or the patient's agent.

decision_logic.condition: A long-term care facility asks for or uses an emergency kit.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the facility type is Board-approved, apply the bed-band caps and packaging of the circular, have a pharmacist seal and reseal within 48 hours after opening, and reconcile dispensed doses.

decision_logic.condition: A hospice inpatient facility asks for on-site acute-use stock.
decision_logic.action: Use an automated dispensing device with a machine-specific Controlled Substance Registration and DEA determination, continuous video, the bed-band caps, single-dose tamper-evident units, pharmacy ownership and reconciliation.

ma_vs_federal.text: Federally a central fill pharmacy returns the filled controlled-substance prescription to the retail pharmacy for delivery to the ultimate user, and Policy 2021-02 likewise sends centrally filled Schedule II-V prescriptions back to the originating pharmacy; the Massachusetts policy's permission for direct shipment reaches only non-reportable Schedule VI drugs, which federal law does not control.

Federal law authorizes a central fill pharmacy through a contract or common owner and state permission; Massachusetts Board policy adds that the central fill pharmacy must hold a Massachusetts resident or non-resident retail pharmacy licence and bars central filling of compounded sterile and complex non-sterile preparations. Where both reach the arrangement, the pharmacy meets both.

The federal central fill marking, record and label rules bind Schedule II-V. For Schedule VI, a Massachusetts category, Policy 2021-02 applies the same handling as Board guidance, except that the phrase "central fill" need not be added.

exceptions.text: A centrally filled Schedule VI drug may be delivered or shipped directly to the patient from the central fill pharmacy, but not a Schedule VI drug that is reported to the Prescription Monitoring Program.
The phrase "central fill" is not required on a Schedule VI prescription, although Schedule VI central filling otherwise follows the DEA handling.
A central fill pharmacy may not prepare a Schedule II prescription on an oral authorization from a retail pharmacist or a practitioner.
247 CMR 9.04(4) on bed-side delivery and 9.04(9) on workplace collection do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.
An institutional pharmacy or a pharmacy department is not a pharmacy for the lock box statute, except as 247 CMR provides.

A long-term care facility may use an automated dispensing device in place of the traditional locked box for Schedule II-V emergency kit stock, provided all relevant regulations and guidance requirements are met.
Neither a long-term care facility nor a hospice inpatient facility is required to stock every listed item or the maximum quantity.

timing_deadlines.event: Original Schedule II prescription transmitted for central fill
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Kept by the retail pharmacy for two years from the date the prescription was filled

timing_deadlines.event: Original Schedule III-V prescription transmitted for central fill
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Kept by the retail pharmacy for two years from the date the prescription was last refilled
timing_deadlines.consequence: Counting from the first fill shortens the period the regulation sets.

timing_deadlines.event: Shared pharmacy services policies and procedures
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Reviewed at least annually, with the review documented
timing_deadlines.consequence: A missing documented review departs from Policy 2021-02 III(o).

timing_deadlines.event: Emergency kit opened in a long-term care facility
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Inspected, re-stocked and resealed by the pharmacist within 48 hours prior to further use
timing_deadlines.consequence: The kit is not to be used again until the pharmacist has done so.

timing_deadlines.event: Transport time-test studies for temperature-sensitive deliveries
timing_deadlines.timeframe: At least twice yearly, summer and winter (recommendation)
timing_deadlines.consequence: The advisory recommends this to ensure stability and safety during transport.

timing_deadlines.event: Hospice acute-use dose supplied from the device
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Only until the pharmacy can fill and deliver the full prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: The acute-use supply is a bridge, not a substitute for filling the prescription.

forms_records.text: Retail pharmacy transmitting a Schedule II-V prescription for central fill: "CENTRAL FILL" written on the face of the original; the central fill pharmacy's name, address and DEA number; the transmitting pharmacist; the date of transmittal (for an electronic Schedule II prescription, added to the electronic record); the refills dispensed and remaining for Schedules III-V; and a receipt record showing the date, the delivery method and the employee who accepted delivery.

Central fill pharmacy: the fax copy or an electronic record of everything transmitted, including the retail pharmacy's name, address and DEA number; the date of receipt, the filling pharmacist and the filling or refilling dates; and the date and method of delivery back to the retail pharmacy.

Both pharmacies keep a list of partner pharmacies with name, address and DEA number and verify each partner's registration, available to DEA on request; the central fill pharmacy's label shows the retail pharmacy's name and address and a unique identifier such as its DEA number.

Shared pharmacy services under Policy 2021-02: a system audit trail showing at least the date, time and individuals at each step; documented training; the written contract or agreement where ownership differs; joint policies and procedures with the annual review documented; a continuity of care plan; and a policy for medications never dispensed.

Mail and common carrier delivery: written policies and procedures for packing, shipping, transporting and delivering controlled substances under 247 CMR 9.02(3); the advisory also recommends documenting the workflow, witnessed controlled substance packaging, tracking numbers, returned and lost packages, and contracted drivers' delivery logs with recipient signatures.

Emergency kits: the pharmacy's policy and procedure on security, maintenance and use and its reconciliation of kit doses with prescriptions or orders; a contents list on the outside cover and inside the kit; and the facility's formulary and accountability procedures.

Hospice acute-use device: a machine-specific Controlled Substance Registration, the pharmacy's determination on a machine-specific DEA number, continuous video monitoring, reconciliation of dispensed doses with prescriptions, and the facility's formulary and accountability procedures subject to review.

role_duties.role: Dispensing pharmacy receiving off-site processed medication
role_duties.duty: Dispense only if the process was verified by a Massachusetts licensed pharmacist or performed in a Board-licensed pharmacy.

role_duties.role: Retail pharmacy in a shared services arrangement
role_duties.duty: Notify patients that another pharmacy may process or fill their prescriptions, provide an opt-out, and share joint responsibility for properly processed and filled prescriptions.

role_duties.role: Originating retail pharmacy using central fill
role_duties.duty: Transmit and annotate the prescription, keep the original and the receipt record, keep the partner list, and make the final dispensing of Schedule II-V and reportable Schedule VI prescriptions.

Hold a Massachusetts retail pharmacy licence, keep its records, label the package with the retail pharmacy's name and address and its own identifier, return Schedule II-V and reportable Schedule VI prescriptions to the originating pharmacy, and not centrally fill sterile or complex non-sterile compounded preparations.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist in a registered central fill pharmacy
role_duties.duty: Fill controlled-substance prescriptions only in the usual course of professional practice, bearing corresponding liability for a prescription not in proper form.

role_duties.role: Board-licensed pharmacy dispensing after telepharmacy verification
role_duties.duty: Have at least one licensed pharmacist on the premises and use verification technology meeting the policy's minimums.
Keep packing, shipping and transport from harming integrity or stability, and maintain controlled substance shipping policies.
Obtain consent, respect freedom of choice, and hand the medications directly to the patient or agent.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist, employee or agent collecting at a workplace
role_duties.duty: Collect in person, hand over directly to the patient or agent, and return everything else to the pharmacy; the pharmacist and pharmacy answer for the agent's conduct.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy registered to dispense Schedule II-V
role_duties.duty: Make lock boxes available for sale at each store and display the required sign on or near the counter.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist supplying a long-term care facility kit
role_duties.duty: Prepare, package and seal the kit with a contents list, and inspect, re-stock and reseal it within 48 hours after opening prior to further use.
Keep a kit policy on security, maintenance and use, reconcile kit doses, and supply only Board-approved facility types.

Provide a kit, use its medications only on a primary care provider's order, keep Schedule II-V within the bed-band caps, and have Schedule VI emergency stock monitored by its Quality Assurance and Assessment Committee.
Use an automated dispensing device with machine-specific registration and DEA determination, keep within the caps, retain ownership until dispensing, and reconcile with prescriptions.

common_traps.text: Treating a pharmacist's inspection of a finished product as verification of off-site processing.
Assuming a signed shared services agreement permits a central fill pharmacy to ship a Schedule II-V prescription straight to the patient.
Reading Schedule VI status as blanket permission for direct shipment, when monitoring-program reportable drugs such as gabapentin are carved out.

Relying on the originating pharmacy's Massachusetts licence to cover an unlicensed out-of-state central fill pharmacy. Board policy requires the central fill pharmacy's own licence; 247 CMR 9.04(11) alone would also accept a Massachusetts pharmacist's verification of the process, but a central fill arrangement that meets only that condition does not meet the policy, so the safe course is a licensed central fill pharmacy.
Having the central fill pharmacy write "CENTRAL FILL" instead of the transmitting retail pharmacy.
Presenting the delivery and shipping advisory's items, such as a delivery signature or twice-yearly time-test studies, as regulatory mandates.
Handing bed-side discharge medications to a unit nurse because the patient consented to the service.
Leaving uncollected workplace deliveries with a site contact rather than returning them to the pharmacy.
Treating long-term care emergency kit caps as per drug or as a pooled total across categories.
Letting facility staff reseal an opened emergency kit, or putting it back in use before the pharmacist has resealed it.
Using acute-use hospice stock as routine floor stock that belongs to the facility.

drug_examples.teaching_point: Policy 2021-02 names gabapentin as a Schedule VI drug reportable to the Prescription Monitoring Program, so a centrally filled gabapentin prescription may not be shipped directly to the patient and goes back to the originating pharmacy.

As a Schedule II controlled substance, a centrally filled morphine prescription must return to the originating pharmacy for final dispensing, and the retail pharmacy keeps the original for two years from the date it was filled.

authority.name: 247 CMR 9.00: Professional Practice Standards

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 9.04(11) a pharmacy may not dispense any medication that was processed outside its licensed pharmacy premises unless said process was verified by a Massachusetts licensed pharmacist or performed in a pharmacy licensed by the Board.

authority.name: 247 CMR 9.00: Professional Practice Standards

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 9.02(1) a pharmacy and pharmacist may dispense prescription drugs by mail or common carrier in a manner consistent with federal and state laws and regulations. Under 9.02(2) a pharmacy shall ensure that packing, shipping, and transportation processes do not adversely affect the integrity or stability of medications dispensed by mail. Under 9.02(3) a pharmacy shall maintain policies and procedures regarding packing, shipping, transporting, and delivering controlled substances.

authority.name: Massachusetts professional practice standards

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 9.04(4), a pharmacy that provides bed-side delivery service of discharge prescriptions to patients in an inpatient healthcare facility must obtain patient consent to provide such services and may not restrict a patient's freedom of choice of pharmacy services. A pharmacy that provides bed-side delivery service shall deliver any medications directly to the patient or the patient's agent.

authority.name: 247 CMR 9.00: Professional Practice Standards

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 9.04(9) a pharmacist or individual acting on behalf of a pharmacy may not collect prescriptions at industrial plants, places of business, or other sites where specific groups of people are regularly employed or affiliated unless all of the following are met: (a) the prescriptions are written for persons regularly employed at, or affiliated with, the site, or for immediate family members living at the same address as such persons; (b) a pharmacist, pharmacy employee, or authorized agent of the pharmacy collects the prescriptions in person; (c) a pharmacist, pharmacy employee, or authorized agent of the pharmacy dispenses the prescription medications directly to the patient or patient's agent; (d) a pharmacist, pharmacy employee, or authorized agent of the pharmacy returns to the pharmacy all prescription medications not dispensed directly to a patient or patient's agent, and prescription medications may not be left or stored at the delivery location; and (e) the pharmacist and pharmacy are responsible for the conduct of any pharmacy employee or authorized agent acting on the pharmacist's behalf. Under 247 CMR 9.04(15) these requirements do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.
exceptions: Under 247 CMR 9.04(15) the requirements of 9.04(9) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

authority.name: 247 CMR 9.00: Professional Practice Standards

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 9.09(1) a pharmacy shall maintain a policy and procedure for the proper dispensing of medication through emergency medication kits pertaining to security, maintenance, and use. Under 9.09(2) a pharmacy shall reconcile medication dispensed through emergency medication kits with prescriptions or orders. Under 9.09(3) a pharmacy may only provide emergency medication kits to types of facilities approved by the Board.

authority.name: Massachusetts General Laws

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 21B(a) defines a lock box as a box with a locking mechanism that cannot be tampered with or opened without extreme force, and a pharmacy as a facility under the direction or supervision of a registered pharmacist which is authorized to dispense controlled substances, provided that pharmacy does not include an institutional pharmacy or a pharmacy department except as otherwise provided in 247 CMR. Under s. 21B(b) a pharmacy registered in the commonwealth to dispense schedule II, III, IV or V prescription drugs shall make available prescription lock boxes for sale at each store location, and pharmacies shall make customers aware of their availability by displaying a sign on or near the pharmacy counter that is at least 4 inches by 5 inches and includes, in legibly printed font, the statement: "Lock boxes for securing your prescription medications are available at this pharmacy".
exceptions: An institutional pharmacy or a pharmacy department is not a pharmacy for s. 21B, except as otherwise provided in 247 CMR.

authority.name: 105 CMR 150.000: Standards for Long-Term Care Facilities

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 105 CMR 150.008(E) an emergency medication kit shall be provided in all long-term care facilities. (1) The contents of the kit shall be approved by the Department; in a SNCFC a pediatric emergency kit and emergency resuscitation equipment and medication shall be provided, with a chart listing pediatric doses for emergency drugs included with the emergency equipment. (2) The kit shall be kept in a separate, sealed container stored in a suitable place when not in use, and drugs requiring refrigeration shall be kept in a separate sealed container under proper refrigeration. (3) Each kit shall be prepared, packaged and sealed by a pharmacist and shall contain a list of contents on the outside cover and within the box. (4) The medications in the kit shall be used only upon the orders of a primary care provider. (5) After a kit has been opened, it shall be inspected, re-stocked and resealed by the pharmacist within 48 hours prior to further use.

authority.name: Board of Registration in Pharmacy Policy 2021-02: Shared Pharmacy Service Models Including Central Fill, Remote Processing, and Telepharmacy (adopted 2/19/21; revised 4/7/22 and 2/6/25)
authority.section: Policy 2021-02, sections I, II and III(a)-(q)

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Board Policy 2021-02 (adopted 2/19/21; revised 4/7/22 and 2/6/25) provides minimum standards for Shared Pharmacy Service models involving Massachusetts licensees, and states that, unless otherwise noted, shared service models not addressed in the policy require a petition to the Board for approval. It adopts the NABP definition of Shared Pharmacy Services: a system that allows a participating pharmacist or pharmacy, pursuant to a request from another participating pharmacist or pharmacy, to process or fill a prescription drug order, which may include preparing, packaging, labeling, compounding for specific patients, dispensing, performing drug utilization reviews, conducting claims adjudication, obtaining refill authorizations, reviewing therapeutic interventions, and/or reviewing institutional facility orders. Its general requirements for all models are that: all participants maintain full compliance with federal and state law, including pharmacy licensure and technician supervision requirements (or the state equivalent); shared services occur within the United States; participants have the same owner or a written contract or agreement outlining the services provided and the shared responsibilities of each party; participants share a common electronic file or technology allowing secure access to required information; participants assure data security and protect the confidentiality and integrity of protected health information; no part of the database is duplicated, downloaded, or removed from the pharmacy's electronic database; dispensed medications are pursuant to valid, patient-specific prescriptions or standing orders; pharmacy systems can track and produce an audit trail of the prescription through each step, including at a minimum date/time and individuals involved; each participant is jointly responsible for properly processed and filled prescriptions; initiation or continuation of therapy, quality, or safety is not compromised; retail pharmacies notify patients that their prescriptions may be processed or filled by another pharmacy and provide a mechanism for patients to opt out; all participants have documented training; participants jointly develop, implement, review, revise and comply with joint policies and procedures, each maintaining the portion relating to its operations and including at a minimum those in the Shared Pharmacy Services section of the most recent NABP Model Act; participants review the written policies and procedures at least annually and document the review; pharmacies establish and maintain a continuity of care plan for when any participant cannot process or fill prescriptions; and participants comply with any other requirements the Board deems necessary to protect public health and safety.

authority.name: Board of Registration in Pharmacy Advisory: Medication Delivery and Shipping (adopted 6/28/18; revised 1/9/25)
authority.section: Full text: General Recommendations; Schedule II-V Controlled Substances; Refrigerated/Frozen/Other Temperature Sensitive Products; Hazardous Products; Delivery to Alternative Locations; Counseling; Unclaimed Products; Lost in Transit; Pharmacies Utilizing Contracted Drivers

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: The Board of Registration in Pharmacy Advisory: Medication Delivery and Shipping (adopted 6/28/18; revised 1/9/25) sets out best practice recommendations that the Board urges all pharmacies to review as a high priority and to consider implementing as appropriate. Its general recommendations are to ensure compliance with federal and state law, including licensure in other states if required; obtain patient consent for delivery or shipping; document the workflow, including verifying the delivery address and product packaging; permit only trained pharmacy personnel to package medications and produce delivery labels; recommend that two employees witness the packaging of controlled substances and maintain documentation; use proper packaging systems, including appropriate containers and tamper resistant tape; and develop quality assurance methods for packaging. For Schedule II-V controlled substances it recommends requiring a signature upon delivery, recording the tracking number, including the pharmacy's address but not its name on the label, and reviewing the Prescription Monitoring Program dispenser guide and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18. For temperature-sensitive products it recommends policies for excursions during delivery, a time-test study at least twice yearly (summer and winter), and packing with a barrier layer between cold packs and the medication and a calibrated temperature monitoring device next to the medication. It also addresses hazardous products, delivery to alternative locations (including that a specialty pharmacy delivering to a retail pharmacy for patient pick-up may do so only if delivering the final packaged product, which the receiving pharmacy may not alter), counseling materials, unclaimed products, packages lost in transit (including reporting lost packages containing federally controlled substances or other drugs with abuse potential to the Board in accordance with its Loss or Theft of Controlled Substances policy), and contracted drivers (including a policy that deliveries are not left at the front desk of an assisted living facility or in the hands of a staff member).

authority.name: Department of Public Health Circular Letter DHCQ 18-6-679: Controlled Substances in Schedule II-V Approved for Inclusion in Long Term Care Facilities Emergency Kits (June 15, 2018)
authority.section: Full text and attached Revised List of Controlled Substances in Schedule II-V Approved for Inclusion in Long-Term Care Facility Emergency Kits

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Department of Public Health Circular Letter DHCQ 18-6-679 (June 15, 2018), jointly issued by the Bureau of Health Care Safety and Quality and the Drug Control Program and Board of Registration in Pharmacy through the Bureau of Health Professions Licensure, attaches the revised list of Schedule II-V controlled substances that long-term care facilities are permitted to store on their premises in a locked emergency kit, and supersedes Circular Letter DHCQ 06-10-467 (October 18, 2006). The list was developed under 105 CMR 150.008(E)(1). Actual contents are determined by each facility within the Department's framework, which allows a choice of federally controlled analgesic and sedative/anticonvulsant medications in Schedules II-V up to a maximum number of units per facility based on licensed bed capacity, in a 3:1 ratio of analgesics to sedatives/anticonvulsants: analgesics (CII-CV) 45 units for <50 beds, 60 for 51-100 beds, 75 for 101-150 beds and 90 for >150 beds; sedatives/anticonvulsants (CII-CV) 15, 20, 25 and 30 units in the same bands. Each facility should develop its own formulary in conjunction with a single pharmacy provider of its own choosing and develop policies and procedures, including measures for controlled substance accountability and security, subject to review; facilities are not required to have all items or the maximum quantity. Each unit must be tamper evident/resistant, in an individually packaged, single dose form. Facilities that wish to store Schedule VI controlled substances for emergency doses must comply with the requirements for procurement, storage, dispensing, administration, recording and disposal of those substances; their storage must comply with facility policies and procedures under 105 CMR 150.008 and with federal and state law, and their use must be monitored by the facility's Quality Assurance and Assessment Committee. DPH approves the use of automated dispensing devices by long-term care facilities in place of the traditional locked boxes for Schedule II-V controlled substances in emergency kits, provided all relevant regulations and guidance requirements are met. Emergency kit practices, policies and procedures may be reviewed at any time by Bureau of Health Care Safety and Quality or Drug Control Program staff.

authority.name: Department of Public Health Circular Letter DHCQ 20-3-700: Schedule II-VI Controlled Substances Approved for Acute Use in Hospice Inpatient Facilities (March 6, 2020)
authority.section: Full text and attached List of Controlled Substances in Schedule II-VI Approved for Inclusion in Hospice Care Acute Use Medications

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Department of Public Health Circular Letter DHCQ 20-3-700 (March 6, 2020), jointly issued by the Bureau of Health Care Safety and Quality and the Board of Registration in Pharmacy through the Bureau of Health Professions Licensure, outlines a process through which an inpatient hospice facility's pharmacy provider is permitted to store certain non-patient specific medications on-site at the hospice facility for patient administration. It attaches a list of Schedule II-VI controlled substances that hospice inpatient facilities, as defined in 105 CMR 141.000, may allow a pharmacy to store on their premises via an automated dispensing device (ADD) for acute use, meaning medications intended to treat patient symptoms that are not life threatening but require use in a timely manner to provide prompt palliative care; the supply should only be enough to treat the patient until the pharmacy can fill and deliver the full prescription. The pharmacy provider must use an ADD to store and secure acute use medications, must obtain a machine-specific Controlled Substance Registration from the Board of Registration in Pharmacy, and must determine whether a machine-specific DEA number is required; in addition to continuous monitoring by video, other ADD requirements are in Board Policy 2019-02. An ADD at an inpatient hospice facility may contain up to, but not more than, the allowed quantity for each category, per facility and based on licensed bed capacity: analgesics (CII-CV) 50 units for <10 beds, 100 for 11-20 beds and 150 for >21 beds; sedatives/anticonvulsants (CII-CV) 30, 60 and 90; ancillary medications (CVI, e.g. antiemetics, antipsychotics) 25, 50 and 75. Facilities are not required to have all items or the maximum quantity; each facility should develop its own formulary with the pharmacy providing the on-site ADD and develop policies and procedures, including controlled substance accountability and security measures, subject to review. The contents of the ADD remain the property of the pharmacy until dispensed for administration pursuant to a prescriber's prescription or order; medications dispensed through the ADD must be reconciled by the pharmacy with prescriptions; and each unit must be tamper evident/resistant, in an individually packaged, single dose form. The facility's acute use practices, policies and procedures may be reviewed at any time by Bureau of Health Care Safety and Quality or Board staff.

authority.name: Definitions
authority.section: 21 CFR 1300.01, definition of Central fill pharmacy

authority.name: Registration of manufacturers, distributors and dispensers
Purpose of issue of prescription; persons entitled to fill prescriptions
Distributions requiring a Form 222 or a digitally signed electronic order; dispensing without prescription

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1300.01 a central fill pharmacy means a pharmacy which is permitted by the state in which it is located to prepare controlled substances orders for dispensing pursuant to a valid prescription transmitted to it by a registered retail pharmacy and to return the labeled and filled prescriptions to the retail pharmacy for delivery to the ultimate user; it is deemed authorized to fill prescriptions on behalf of a retail pharmacy only if the retail pharmacy and central fill pharmacy have a contractual relationship providing for such activities or share a common owner. The registration table in 21 CFR 1301.13(e)(1) places Central Fill Pharmacy within the dispensing or instructing business activity for Schedules II-V and states that a retail pharmacy may perform central fill pharmacy activities. Under 21 CFR 1306.06 a prescription for a controlled substance may only be filled by a pharmacist acting in the usual course of professional practice and either registered individually or employed in a registered pharmacy, a registered central fill pharmacy, or a registered institutional practitioner, and under 21 CFR 1306.05(f) the corresponding liability for filling a prescription not prepared in the form DEA regulations prescribe rests on the pharmacist, including a pharmacist employed by a central fill pharmacy. Under 21 CFR 1305.03(d) delivery from a central fill pharmacy to a retail pharmacy does not require a DEA Form 222 or electronic order, and under 21 CFR 1306.26(g) central fill pharmacies may not dispense controlled substances to a purchaser at retail under that section.

authority.name: Board of Registration in Pharmacy Policy 2021-02: Shared Pharmacy Service Models Including Central Fill, Remote Processing, and Telepharmacy (adopted 2/19/21; revised 4/7/22 and 2/6/25)

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Section V of Board Policy 2021-02 (adopted 2/19/21; revised 4/7/22 and 2/6/25) defines remote processing services as a system that allows the processing of patient-specific prescriptions outside the licensed pharmacy premises of a Massachusetts-licensed pharmacy without final product verification or dispensing responsibilities, and states that prescriptions may be processed outside those premises provided the processes are verified by a Massachusetts-licensed pharmacist or performed in a pharmacy licensed by the Board. A note adds that, in accordance with the Board's Scope of Practice policy, pharmacy technicians holding a Massachusetts pharmacy technician license may perform remote processing on behalf of a retail or institutional pharmacy located in Massachusetts without on-site supervision by a Massachusetts-licensed pharmacist. Section VI defines telepharmacy as the utilization of telecommunications technology to oversee aspects of pharmacy operations or provide patient care services, and limits the telepharmacy the policy allows to remote pharmacist verification of final patient-specific products and clinical activities by a pharmacist such as patient counseling, drug utilization review, and drug therapy monitoring. Telepharmacy activities must be conducted by a Massachusetts-licensed pharmacist or performed in a Board-licensed pharmacy; the Board-licensed pharmacy dispensing the final patient-specific product must have at least one licensed pharmacist on the premises; and technologies used for remote verification must be in good working order with, at a minimum, high definition image resolution with variable viewing options and sufficient data retention capabilities to investigate quality-related events.

authority.name: Board of Registration in Pharmacy Policy 2021-02: Shared Pharmacy Service Models Including Central Fill, Remote Processing, and Telepharmacy (adopted 2/19/21; revised 4/7/22 and 2/6/25)

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Section IV of Board Policy 2021-02 (adopted 2/19/21; revised 4/7/22 and 2/6/25) states that retail pharmacies licensed by the Board may serve as central fill pharmacies for other Board-licensed retail pharmacies, and a central fill pharmacy may provide central filling for one or more pharmacies. When one retail pharmacy receives a prescription and a second pharmacy prepares and subsequently delivers the filled prescription to the first retail pharmacy for dispensing to the patient, the second pharmacy is engaging in central fill activity; the policy refers readers to the full DEA definition and requirements for a central fill pharmacy. Its requirements are: (i) any central fill pharmacy dispensing medications into, within, or from Massachusetts to participating pharmacies must be licensed by Massachusetts as a resident or non-resident retail pharmacy; (ii) participating pharmacies that dispense federally controlled substances (Schedules II-V) must follow DEA regulations for central fill pharmacies and be registered with DEA, and, except as noted, must handle the central filling of Massachusetts Schedule VI controlled substances in the same manner as the DEA regulations outline for Schedule II-V, although the phrase "central fill" is not required to be added to Schedule VI prescriptions; (iii) centrally filled Schedule II-V controlled substances must be delivered to the pharmacy where the prescription originated for final dispensing to the patient; (iv) centrally filled Schedule VI controlled substances, with the exception of drugs (i.e., gabapentin) requiring reporting to the Prescription Monitoring Program, may be delivered or shipped directly to the patient from the central fill pharmacy; (v) the central filling of compounded sterile preparations or complex non-sterile preparations to be dispensed into, within, or from Massachusetts is prohibited; and (vi) participants must maintain a policy and procedure regarding the handling of medications that have not been dispensed to patients.
exceptions: Centrally filled Schedule VI drugs may be delivered or shipped directly to the patient from the central fill pharmacy, except drugs (i.e., gabapentin) requiring reporting to the Prescription Monitoring Program.
The phrase "central fill" is not required to be added to Schedule VI prescriptions, although Schedule VI central filling is otherwise handled as the DEA regulations outline for Schedule II-V.

authority.name: Provision of prescription information between retail pharmacies and central fill pharmacies for prescriptions of Schedule II controlled substances
Provision of prescription information between retail pharmacies and central fill pharmacies for initial and refill prescriptions of Schedule III, IV, or V controlled substances

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1306.15 (Schedule II) and 21 CFR 1306.27 (Schedules III, IV and V) a retail pharmacy may provide prescription information to an authorized central fill pharmacy for dispensing purposes, and may transmit the prescriptions electronically, including via facsimile. The transmitting retail pharmacy must write the words "CENTRAL FILL" on the face of the original prescription (1306.15(a)(1) says the original paper prescription) and record the name, address and DEA registration number of the central fill pharmacy, the name of the retail pharmacy pharmacist transmitting the prescription, and the date of transmittal; for an electronic Schedule II prescription, 1306.15(a)(1) requires that information to be added to the electronic prescription record. It must ensure that all information required on a prescription by 21 CFR 1306.05 is transmitted; for Schedules III-V it must also indicate the number of refills already dispensed and the number remaining. It must maintain the original prescription for two years from the date the prescription was filled (Schedule II) or last refilled (Schedules III-V), and keep a record of receipt of the filled prescription, including the date of receipt, the method of delivery (private, common or contract carrier) and the name of the retail pharmacy employee accepting delivery. The central fill pharmacy must keep a copy of the prescription (if sent via facsimile) or an electronic record of all information transmitted, including the name, address and DEA registration number of the transmitting retail pharmacy; a record of the date of receipt, the name of the pharmacist (for Schedules III-V, the licensed pharmacist) filling the prescription, and the date of filling (for Schedules III-V, dates of filling or refilling); and a record of the date the filled prescription was delivered to the retail pharmacy and the method of delivery.

authority.name: Labeling of substances and filling of prescriptions
Records of authorized central fill pharmacies and retail pharmacies

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1306.14(b) (Schedule II) and 21 CFR 1306.24(b) (Schedules III, IV and V), if the prescription is filled at a central fill pharmacy, the central fill pharmacy shall affix to the package a label showing the retail pharmacy name and address and a unique identifier (i.e. the central fill pharmacy's DEA registration number) indicating that the prescription was filled at the central fill pharmacy, in addition to the label information required by paragraph (a) of each section. Under 21 CFR 1304.05(a) every retail pharmacy that utilizes the services of a central fill pharmacy must keep a record of all central fill pharmacies, including name, address and DEA number, authorized to fill prescriptions on its behalf, and must verify the registration of each; under 1304.05(b) every central fill pharmacy must keep a record of all retail pharmacies, including name, address and DEA number, for which it is authorized to fill prescriptions, and must verify the registration of each. These records must be made available upon request for inspection by DEA.

authority.name: Emergency oral Schedule II records and follow-up handling

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(2) the emergency oral Schedule II prescription SHALL BE IMMEDIATELY REDUCED TO WRITING BY THE PHARMACIST and shall contain all information 21 CFR 1306.05 requires EXCEPT the prescribing individual practitioner's signature. Under 1306.11(d)(4) the follow-up prescription must bear on its face 'AUTHORIZATION FOR EMERGENCY DISPENSING' AND THE DATE OF THE ORAL ORDER; it may be delivered in person or by mail, but a mailed paper prescription MUST BE POSTMARKED WITHIN THE 7-DAY PERIOD; UPON RECEIPT the dispensing pharmacist MUST ATTACH the paper prescription to the oral emergency prescription earlier reduced to writing, and for an ELECTRONIC follow-up must ANNOTATE the electronic prescription record with the original authorization and the date of the oral order. FAILURE OF THE PHARMACIST to notify the nearest DEA office when the practitioner does not deliver the follow-up SHALL VOID THE AUTHORITY conferred by 1306.11(d) to dispense without a written prescription. Under 1306.11(d)(5) a central fill pharmacy is not authorized to prepare a Schedule II prescription on an oral authorization from a retail pharmacist or practitioner.
exceptions: A mailed follow-up satisfies the period by its postmark, not by the date the pharmacy receives it.
An electronic follow-up is annotated rather than physically attached.
The central fill prohibition in 1306.11(d)(5) removes the emergency oral route entirely for that setting.

authority.name: Other security controls for practitioners

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: The registrant shall notify the Field Division Office of the Administration in his area, in writing, of the theft or significant loss of any controlled substances within one business day of discovery of such loss or theft, and must also file a complete and accurate DEA Form 106 with the Administration through DEA's Diversion Control Division secure network application within 45 days after discovery of the theft or loss. In determining whether a loss is significant a registrant should consider, among others, the actual quantity lost in relation to the type of business; the specific controlled substances lost; whether the loss can be associated with access by specific individuals or attributed to unique activities; a pattern of losses over a specific time period, whether the losses appear random, and the results of efforts taken to resolve them; and, if known, whether the substances are likely candidates for diversion and local trends and other indicators of diversion potential. Where a retail pharmacy contracts with private, common or contract carriers to retrieve filled prescriptions from a central fill pharmacy, the retail pharmacy is responsible for reporting in-transit losses upon discovery by use of a DEA Form 106.

authority.name: 247 CMR 9.00: Professional Practice Standards

rule_dependencies.rule_summary: Under 247 CMR 9.04(15), the requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(4), (5), (6), (9), (10), (12), (13) and (14) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies. The excluded requirements include the counting rule in 9.04(10), under which a pharmacist deciding whether a prescription is within date counts the day after the prescription was written as day one; the Schedule VI rule in 9.04(12), under which a Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue and may not be refilled after one year; the Schedule V rule in 9.04(13), under which a Schedule V prescription may not be filled or refilled more than six months after issue or refilled more than five times; and the refill record in 9.04(6), under which a pharmacist refilling a Schedule III-VI prescription records the date of dispensing, the amount dispensed and his or her initials.
